title: What is Atomisation?
author: Kris Boulton
summary: In the launch post of his new newsletter, Kris Boulton introduces three kinds of atomisation -- routine, factual, and conceptual -- starting with routine atomisation, which he applies to what he calls 'cognitive routines': step-by-step processes like expanding brackets or finding the area of a shape. He argues that the dominant teaching model, worked-example problem pairs (popularized by John Sweller and further spread via Doug Lemov's 'I do, We do, You do'), manages cognitive load better than minimally-guided discovery learning but still hits a hard limit, leaving some students overloaded and confused. His proposed solution is to break a cognitive routine down into its constituent 'atoms' -- each one a categorical concept, transformation concept, fact, or another cognitive routine -- which lets a teacher precisely diagnose which specific atom a struggling student hasn't learned, and teach that atom in isolation. Working through finding the area of a trapezium, Boulton shows that most of the six atoms involved are usually not new to students, and identifies atom 3 (selecting which lengths from a diagram are needed) as what he calls a 'plutonium atom' -- the single atom where the real difficulty, and the real leverage, lies.
points: Boulton's core diagnostic claim: 'I do, We do, You do' problem pairs manage cognitive load better than discovery learning but still hit a hard limit, leaving some students overloaded -- atomisation is his proposed fix for that specific residual gap.

His method of atomising a cognitive routine (list every mental step, classify each as a concept, fact, or sub-routine) gives teachers 'X-ray vision' into exactly which step a student is struggling with, rather than a vague sense that 'they don't get it.'

The trapezium-area worked example shows that of six identified atoms, only two (the area formula and selecting the correct lengths) are typically new to students -- meaning most instructional time should target those two, not the whole process from scratch.

Boulton's 'plutonium atom' concept -- singling out atom 3 (selecting the correct lengths) as the atom where all the power and risk lies -- flags that traditional worksheets, which pre-select the needed lengths for students, never actually give practice at the hardest and most consequential step.
quotes: There are three kinds of atomisation. Routine Atomisation. Factual Atomisation. Conceptual Atomisation.
However, I do / We do problem pairs hit a hard limit for managing cognitive load, and so they still leave many children overloaded.
You can see what exactly is new learning for students, or exactly where they are struggling (this is like having X-Ray vision on students’ struggles!)
Traditional worksheets tend to give students only the three lengths they need... so they never get to practise selecting the correct three lengths.
This is an example of what I call a plutonium atom, the atom where all the power lies, something that will transform the end result, and increase their odds of success.
